questions.question: What does it mean for two sets $A$ and $B$ to have the same cardinality?
options: The sets have exactly the same elements.
There exists a bijection $f\colon A\to B$.
One set is a subset of the other.
There exists any function $f\colon A\to B$.
questions.explanation: Two sets A and B have the same cardinality when there exists a bijection f: A -> B (a one-to-one correspondence).
questions.source_support: Definition of equal cardinality by existence of a bijection.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: Having the same elements means A = B (equality), not just same cardinality.
One being a subset of the other does not imply same cardinality.
Any function is too weak; a bijection (injective + surjective) is needed.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: For a finite set, what is its cardinality?
options: The largest element of the set.
The number of its distinct elements.
The number of possible subsets only.
The number of functions from the set to itself.
questions.explanation: For a finite set, cardinality is the number of its distinct elements.
questions.source_support: Definition states that finite-set cardinality is the number of distinct elements.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: The largest element is about ordering, not cardinality.
The number of subsets is 2^n (power set size), not the cardinality.
The number of functions from the set to itself is n^n, not the cardinality.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: What is the cardinality of the finite set $\{2,\,4,\,6\}$?
questions.explanation: The set {2,4,6} has 3 distinct elements, so its cardinality is 3.
questions.source_support: Finite-set cardinality counts distinct elements.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: 1 is too few (there are 3 elements).
2 is too few; the set {2,4,6} has 3 distinct elements.
6 is an element, not the count.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: Which set has the same cardinality as $\{1,\,2,\,3\}$?

questions.question: Cardinality compares the sizes of two sets by means of what?
options: Compare sets by the names of their elements.
Compare sets only by their smallest element.
Compare sets only when both are subsets of $\mathbb{R}$.
questions.explanation: Cardinality compares set sizes through one-to-one correspondences (bijections).
questions.source_support: Cardinality is compared using one-to-one correspondences.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: Element names are irrelevant to cardinality.
The smallest element is about ordering, not cardinality.
Cardinality applies to all sets, not only subsets of R.

questions.question: How are finite sets classified by cardinality?
options: By whether their elements are ordered.
questions.explanation: Finite sets are classified by cardinality using natural numbers (0, 1, 2, ...).

questions.question: Let $A = \{1,\,2\}$ and $B = \{x,\,y\}$. If $f(1) = x$ and $f(2) = y$, what does this show?
questions.explanation: f(1)=x, f(2)=y is a bijection from A={1,2} to B={x,y}, showing A and B have the same cardinality.
questions.source_support: Definition uses a bijection to establish equal cardinality.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: A and B have the same cardinality, but they are not equal (different elements).
B is not a subset of A (they have different types of elements).
A and B have the SAME cardinality, not different.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: Suppose $|A| = |B|$ and $A$ is a finite set with five distinct elements. What can be concluded about $B$?
options: $B$ must contain the same elements as $A$.
questions.explanation: If |A|=|B| and A has 5 distinct elements, then B also has 5 distinct elements (same cardinality).
questions.source_support: Finite cardinality counts distinct elements and equal cardinality is defined by bijection.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: B need not contain the same elements as A (cardinality is about count, not identity).

Equal cardinality means a bijection exists between $A$ and $B$, not that $B\subseteq A$; $B$ may be disjoint from $A$, e.g. $A=\{1,2,3,4,5\}$ and $B=\{6,7,8,9,10\}$ both have five elements yet $B\nsubseteq A$.
B has 5 elements (finite), not infinite.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: Can two infinite sets have different cardinalities?
options: All infinite sets have different cardinalities.
All infinite sets have the same cardinality.
Infinite sets may have equal or different cardinalities.
Infinite sets cannot be compared by cardinality.
questions.explanation: Infinite sets may have equal or different cardinalities (e.g. N and Q have the same cardinality, but N and R do not).
questions.skill_detail: infinite sets can differ in size
questions.source_support: Cardinality compares set sizes, including infinite ones.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: Not all infinite sets have different cardinalities (N and Q are the same).
Not all infinite sets have the same cardinality (N and R differ).
Infinite sets CAN be compared by cardinality (that is the point).

questions.question: What is the cardinality of the empty set, $|\varnothing|$?
questions.explanation: The cardinality of the empty set is 0 (it has no elements).

option_explanations: 1 is wrong; the empty set has 0 elements.

The empty set is finite (0 elements), not infinite.

questions.question: If $|A|=|B|$, does $|B|=|A|$ also hold?
questions.explanation: Yes, |B|=|A| follows from |A|=|B| because the inverse of a bijection is again a bijection.
questions.source_support: Same cardinality is defined by the existence of a bijection.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: Cardinality IS symmetric (if A ~ B then B ~ A).
Symmetry holds for all sets, not only finite ones.
Symmetry holds without requiring A = B.

questions.question: A bijection witnessing $|A|=|B|$ must be:

questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: Injective only is not enough (some elements of B may be missed).
Surjective only is not enough (some elements of A may collide).
A constant function is neither injective nor surjective (for |A| > 1).

questions.question: For finite sets $A$ and $B$, what is $|A\times B|$?
questions.explanation: For finite sets A and B, |A x B| = |A| * |B| (the Cartesian product has |A| times |B| elements).
questions.source_support: Cardinality of a finite set counts its elements.
